what_its_for: Raloxifene is used to treat and prevent osteoporosis (thinning and weakening of bones) in women who have gone through menopause. It works like estrogen in your bones to help keep them strong and reduce the chance of fractures. It is also used to lower the risk of breast cancer in certain postmenopausal women who are at higher risk.
how_to_take: Take raloxifene by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it at any time of day, but try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Make sure you are also getting enough calcium and vitamin D in your diet or through supplements, as your doctor recommends.
dosing: The usual dose is one 60 mg tablet taken once a day. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on that same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store raloxifene at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Do not take raloxifene if you are pregnant, may become pregnant, or are breastfeeding — it can seriously harm an unborn or nursing baby. Avoid long periods of sitting or lying still, such as during long car rides or airplane flights, because raloxifene can increase your risk of dangerous blood clots. If you need to have surgery or will be on bed rest, talk to your doctor — you may need to stop this medicine temporarily. Avoid smoking and limit alcohol, as these can further weaken your bones.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you notice: pain, swelling, or redness in your leg (possible blood clot); sudden shortness of breath or chest pain (possible blood clot in the lung); sudden changes in vision; sudden severe headache; or numbness or weakness on one side of your body. Also call your doctor if you notice new breast lumps or pain, unusual vaginal bleeding, or severe leg cramps. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, especially blood thinners like warfarin.
when_it_works: Raloxifene begins working in your body right away, but it may take several months to a few years before you notice the full benefit on your bone strength. Your doctor will likely order bone density tests from time to time to check how well the medicine is working. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel fine.
special_populations: This medicine is only for postmenopausal women and should NOT be taken by men, children, or women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. If you have a history of blood clots, liver problems, or kidney disease, tell your doctor before starting this medicine, as it may not be safe for you. Older women on bed rest or with limited mobility should use extra caution due to the increased blood clot risk.
